QF.id: Income, Residential Status, Five Heads of Income_10

question.text: Which of the following conditions makes a Resident individual an RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident)?

answer.text: The individual has been resident in India for 9 out of 10 preceding previous years
The individual has been a non-resident in India in 9 out of the 10 preceding previous years
The individual has stayed 730 or more days in India during the 7 preceding previous years
The individual's Indian income exceeds Rs.15 lakh and he has stayed 182 days in India

explanation.text: The Logic: A Resident qualifies as RNOR if ANY ONE of the following is satisfied: (a) non-resident in India in 9 out of 10 preceding previous years, OR (b) total stay in India of 729 days or less in the 7 preceding previous years. Option B correctly states the NR-in-9/10-years condition. Option A reverses it (resident in 9/10 — that condition makes a person ROR, not RNOR). Option C states 730+ days — the RNOR threshold is 729 days or less. Option D describes a basic-residency condition, not an RNOR condition. The Trap: The 9-out-of-10 test is frequently reversed by examiners — "resident in 9/10" vs "non-resident in 9/10" are opposites. Similarly, candidates confuse "729 or less" with "730 or more". Note: RNOR status narrows the scope of taxable income compared with ROR. However, an RNOR is still taxed on foreign income derived from a business controlled from India or a profession set up in India; only other foreign income is outside the Indian tax net during RNOR years.
